summary: The Al-6 sample is the Fe30Mn6Al1C low-density steel (Fe–0.99C–29.48Mn–5.98Al, balance Fe), i.e. the lowest-Al member of the Fe30Mn(x)Al1C series (x = 6–12% Al at ~1% C and 30% Mn) designed to quantify how C, Mn and Al alloying content control the microstructure and mechanical properties of Fe–Mn–Al–C low-density steels. After vacuum induction melting, homogenization at 1200 °C/5 h and hot rolling to 16 mm rods, the material was solution-treated at 1050 °C for 2 h and water quenched. In this state it is a fully austenitic, ferrite-free and κ-carbide-free steel that combines a moderate yield strength with the highest ductility and the highest Charpy impact toughness (−40 °C) of all the steels studied, making it the reference case for the carbide-free end of the alloy design space.
composition: Nominal composition Fe30Mn6Al1C, measured as Fe–0.99C–29.48Mn–5.98Al (bal. Fe), all in mass%. It belongs to the Fe30Mn(x)Al1C ternary series in which Al is varied from 6 to 12% at approximately 1% C and 30% Mn, so that Al is the only deliberate variable relative to the shared reference composition Fe30Mn11Al1C. Al is added as the principal light element for weight reduction (Al has the steepest density-lowering effect per mass% in these steels), while Mn (≈30%) is used to stabilise the FCC austenite and C (≈1%) provides interstitial strengthening; the low Al level applied here means the alloy retains the highest measured density of the Al series (7.12 g/cm³).
processing: The alloy was fabricated in the laboratory by high-frequency vacuum induction melting in a 50 kg capacity furnace, followed by casting into an ingot 150 mm in diameter. The ingot was homogenized at 1200 °C for 5 h and then hot rolled into rods 16 mm in diameter, which were air-cooled to room temperature (parent hot-rolled process). The hot-rolled rod was finally solution-treated at 1050 °C for 2 h followed by water quenching; this 1050 °C–2 h–WQ state defines the sample studied here. For comparison, Al-containing steels were also solution-treated at 1100 °C for 2 h with water quenching (not the state of this sample).
microstructure: After solution treatment at 1050 °C/2 h/WQ the Al-6 steel consists of a single-phase FCC austenite (γ) matrix with equiaxed grains and no BCC ferrite; Table 3 reports no ferrite fraction (f_Bcc = "–") for this composition. The average austenite grain size is 34.2 ± 1.1 μm (EBSD, 15° boundary criterion), the largest among the Al series and consistent with the ferrite-free character of the alloy (small amounts of ferrite, when present, refine the austenite grains). The microstructure contains abundant annealing twin boundaries (Σ3), with a twin-boundary fraction f_Tw = 45.3%. TEM dark-field imaging and SAED along [001]γ show no κ-carbide reflections, i.e. κ-carbides are absent (D_κ-carbides = 0) in this composition; according to the paper's footnote this also implies negligible hardening from any very fine carbide/short-range-ordering features. Across the Al series, κ-carbides appear only at ≥10% Al and coarsen strongly with increasing Al (up to 15 nm at 12% Al), so the absence of carbides in Al-6 reflects its low Al content.
properties: Tensile behaviour (ambient temperature, initial strain rate 1.1×10⁻³ s⁻¹, round specimen with 25 mm gauge length and 5 mm gauge diameter, tensile axis parallel to the rod axis; average of two solution-treated specimens): yield strength 433 ± 5 MPa, ultimate tensile strength 852 ± 1 MPa, uniform elongation 72 ± 0 %, total elongation to failure 73.5 ± 1 %. The maximum work-hardening rate of the 6% Al steel is ~2100 MPa, the highest of the Al series. Derived true-stress parameters: maximum true stress just before necking (σTS) = 1410 MPa and fracture strength (FRS) = 2113 MPa. Impact toughness: Charpy V-notch energy at −40 °C = 354 ± 16 J (specimen 55 mm long, 10 × 10 mm cross-section, 2 mm deep V-notch perpendicular to the rod axis; MTS impact tester, 500 J capacity), the highest value of all designed low-density steels. Density: 7.12 g/cm³ measured by the Archimedes drainage method. Characterization techniques applied to this sample: EBSD on a field-emission-gun SEM (FEI Quanta 650, 20 kV, 0.5 μm step, Channel 5 post-processing, linear intercept grain sizing, specimens electro-polished in 7% Nital), TEM dark-field imaging with SAED (Tecnai G2 F20 S-TWIN, 200 kV; twin-jet electro-polished foils in 10% perchloric acid + 90% ethanol, 20 V, −20 °C), uniaxial tensile testing on an MTS machine, Charpy impact testing on an MTS impact tester, and Archimedes density measurement.
mechanisms: Composition → microstructure: with the lowest Al content (5.98%) in the Fe30Mn(x)Al1C series, the Al-6 steel contains no ferrite and no κ-carbides; because no ferrite phase is available to pin/refine the austenite and no carbides pin the matrix, austenite grains coarsen to the largest size of the Al series (34.2 ± 1.1 μm), in contrast to the ferrite-containing Al-12 steel (12.6 μm).

κ-carbide absence → low yield strength: the κ-carbides in these alloys are coherent with the austenite (confirmed by SAED) and strengthen it by a particle-shear mechanism described by σ_shear = α f^1/2 d_Car^1/2; with D_κ-carbides = 0 the shear contribution vanishes, so the Al-6 steel sits at the low-strength end of the linear relation Rp0.2 = 478 + 97.1 d_Car^0.5, its 433 MPa yield strength being essentially the baseline flow stress from solid-solution hardening plus austenite grain-size strengthening.

Coarse κ-carbides suppress work hardening: shearing of κ-carbides by dislocations is accompanied by easy glide of dislocations across the carbide shear planes, which weakens the work-hardening capacity; this explains why the maximum work-hardening rate falls with increasing κ-carbide size, and why the carbide-free Al-6 steel (lowest Al) retains the highest work-hardening rate (~2100 MPa), enabling its very large uniform elongation of 72%.

κ-carbide size controls toughness: Charpy impact energy at −40 °C decreases steeply with the square root of κ-carbide size (near-zero for d_Car^0.5 > 2 nm^1/2); because the Al-6 steel is carbide-free, its austenitic FCC matrix delivers the highest toughness measured (354 ± 16 J), while precipitates in the higher Al/C alloys embrittle them.

Constant σTS and σFS: the maximum true stress just before necking (≈1350 MPa on average; 1410 MPa for Al-6) and the fracture strength (≈2150 MPa on average; 2113 MPa for Al-6) are nearly independent of C, Mn and Al content and of the large variations in ferrite fraction, austenite grain size and κ-carbide size; this implies that crack nucleation and final fracture strength are controlled by a mechanism insensitive to these microstructural parameters, which the authors leave to be clarified in future work.

Solution temperature → grain size → strength: raising the solution-treatment temperature from 1050 to 1100 °C slightly lowers the yield strength of the Al-containing steels, which is attributed to austenite grain growth at the higher temperature, whereas the work-hardening-rate ordering (6% Al highest) is preserved.
conclusions: Within the Fe30Mn(x)Al1C family, the low-Al, ferrite-free and κ-carbide-free Al-6 composition represents the ductile/tough extreme of the alloy design space: it shows the highest total elongation (73.5%) and the highest Charpy impact toughness at −40 °C (354 ± 16 J) of all thirteen designed low-density steels, at the expense of the lowest yield strength (433 MPa) of the Al series and the highest density (7.12 g/cm³). This sample anchors the paper's central structure–property finding that the κ-carbide size, rather than austenite grain size, ferrite volume fraction or twin-boundary fraction, governs strength (yield strength ∝ d_Car^0.5), ductility (elongation and area reduction decrease linearly with d_Car^0.5) and impact toughness in solution-treated Fe–Mn–Al–C low-density steels; because κ-carbide size is controlled by C and Al content, alloy design for high strength plus high ductility and toughness can proceed by tuning the carbide size through composition. The paper notes that only three of the designed steels retained high toughness (Fe30Mn6Al1C 354 J, Fe30Mn8Al1C 294 J, Fe30Mn10Al1C 237 J) and that an excellent combination of 642 MPa yield strength, 72% elongation and 247 J impact toughness at 6.69 g/cm³ was achieved in the Fe30Mn10Al1C steel; in addition, the density of these steels is described by ρ = 8.1–0.102C–0.10Al–0.01Mn (mass%), which reproduces measured values far better than the previously published coefficient for C.
unmapped: For the 6% Al steel the text reports a grain size of 33.4 μm ('not shown in Fig. 5'), whereas Table 3 lists 34.2 ± 1.1 μm; the two values differ slightly.

The paper notes that stress–strain jumps after yielding in the tensile curves (Fig. 2) are caused by removal of the extensometer to allow tests to continue to large plastic strain, and do not affect the mechanical property measurements or the work-hardening-rate calculations.

The sample was tested as two solution-treated specimens per condition, with all reported tensile and Charpy values given as averages of two measurements; σTS and FRS are single values derived from Eqns. (1) and (2) using the engineering fracture stress and maximum area reduction.
